question: Does Georgia law dictate whether a broker and an affiliated licensee must structure their relationship as employer-employee or as independent contractor?
choice_a: No -- O.C.G.A. § 43-40-30.1 is statutorily neutral, leaving the choice to the discretion of the broker and licensee
choice_b: Yes -- Georgia law mandates an independent-contractor relationship for all licensees
choice_c: Yes -- Georgia law mandates an employer-employee relationship for all licensees
choice_d: Yes -- the classification is fixed by whichever structure the licensee used at their prior firm
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 43-40-30.1 states that nothing in Chapter 43-40 establishes an employer-employee or broker-independent-contractor relationship between licensees; that determination is left to the licensees' own discretion.

question: A qualifying broker and a newly affiliated salesperson want to formalize their working arrangement. Which statement correctly reflects O.C.G.A. § 43-40-30.1?
choice_a: GREC must approve the classification in writing before the licensee can begin working
choice_b: The chapter does not establish an employer-employee or broker-independent-contractor relationship between them; that determination is left to the licensees themselves
choice_c: The classification automatically defaults to employer-employee unless the broker files a waiver
choice_d: Only firms organized as corporations may choose independent-contractor status
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 43-40-30.1 leaves the employer-employee versus independent-contractor determination entirely to the discretion of the broker and licensee, with no GREC approval process or entity-type restriction.

question: Under O.C.G.A. § 43-40-25(b)(7), what unfair trade practice involves a licensee representing a broker other than the one holding the licensee's license?
choice_a: Doing so is permitted freely as long as the transaction closes successfully
choice_b: Doing so is permitted only for commercial, not residential, transactions
choice_c: Doing so without the knowledge and consent of the broker who actually holds the licensee's license
choice_d: Doing so is only a violation if compensation is also involved
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 43-40-25(b)(7) makes it an unfair trade practice to represent a broker other than the one holding your license, without that broker's knowledge and consent.

question: A salesperson licensed under Broker A tells a client she represents Broker B's firm on a listing, without Broker A's knowledge or consent. Has the salesperson committed an unfair trade practice under Georgia law?
choice_a: No -- a licensee may represent any broker at any time without restriction
choice_b: No -- this is only a problem if Broker B is unlicensed
choice_c: Yes, but only because the transaction was residential rather than commercial
choice_d: Yes -- representing a broker other than the one holding her license, without that broker's knowledge and consent, is an enumerated unfair trade practice under O.C.G.A. § 43-40-25(b)(7)
explanation: Because the salesperson represented Broker B without Broker A's (her actual licensing broker's) knowledge and consent, she has violated O.C.G.A. § 43-40-25(b)(7).

question: From whom must a Georgia licensee ordinarily accept commission or compensation for licensed activities?
choice_a: From the broker holding the licensee's license -- accepting compensation from anyone else without that broker's consent is an unfair trade practice under O.C.G.A. § 43-40-25(b)(8)
choice_b: From whichever party to the transaction the licensee prefers
choice_c: Directly from any cooperating broker involved in the deal, without restriction
choice_d: From GREC directly, which then forwards payment to the licensee
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 43-40-25(b)(8) makes it an unfair trade practice to accept commission or compensation from anyone other than the broker holding the licensee's license, without that broker's consent.

question: A listing agent's cooperating broker on the other side of a deal offers to pay the listing agent's commission share directly to the listing agent, bypassing the listing agent's own broker. The listing agent's broker has not consented to this arrangement. Is this permissible under Georgia law?
choice_a: Yes -- licensees may always accept payment directly from a cooperating broker
choice_b: No -- accepting compensation from someone other than the licensee's own broker without that broker's consent is an unfair trade practice under O.C.G.A. § 43-40-25(b)(8)
choice_c: Yes, as long as the amount matches what was disclosed in the listing agreement
choice_d: No, but only because the payment was made in cash rather than by check
explanation: Because the listing agent's own broker has not consented, accepting the direct payment from the cooperating broker violates O.C.G.A. § 43-40-25(b)(8), regardless of payment form or amount.

question: Under O.C.G.A. § 43-40-25(b)(17), is paying commission or compensation to an unlicensed person for performing licensee services generally treated as an unfair trade practice in Georgia?
choice_a: No -- brokers may pay any unlicensed assistant for any service performed
choice_b: No -- this provision applies only to salespersons, not brokers
choice_c: Yes, as a general rule, subject to a few narrow statutory carve-outs
choice_d: Yes, but only if the unlicensed person is a family member of the licensee
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 43-40-25(b)(17) generally treats paying compensation to anyone performing licensee services who is not properly licensed as an unfair trade practice, subject to a few narrow enumerated carve-outs.

question: Under the carve-outs to O.C.G.A. § 43-40-25(b)(17), may commission be paid to an unlicensed person in connection with a deceased licensee's earned commission?
choice_a: No -- once a licensee dies, any commission they earned is forfeited entirely
choice_b: No -- the commission must instead be paid to GREC for deposit into the Recovery Fund
choice_c: Yes, but only if the estate itself obtains a real estate license within 30 days
choice_d: Yes -- payment to the estate or heirs of a licensee who was validly licensed when the commission was earned is a recognized carve-out
explanation: One of the narrow carve-outs to O.C.G.A. § 43-40-25(b)(17) permits payment to the estate or heirs of a deceased licensee who was validly licensed when the commission was earned.

question: Which of the following is one of the narrow carve-outs to Georgia's general prohibition on paying unlicensed persons under O.C.G.A. § 43-40-25(b)(17)?
choice_a: A referral agent from a foreign, non-licensing country, provided specified evidentiary conditions are met
choice_b: Any unlicensed office manager who schedules showings
choice_c: Any unlicensed marketing consultant hired by the firm
choice_d: Any unlicensed relative of the qualifying broker
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 43-40-25(b)(17) carves out payment to a foreign referral agent from a non-licensing country when specified evidentiary conditions are met -- a narrow exception, not a general allowance for unlicensed staff.

question: Under a carve-out to O.C.G.A. § 43-40-25(b)(17), may a firm pay compensation to an unlicensed business entity in connection with a licensee's earned commission?
choice_a: No -- payment must always be made directly to the individual licensee personally, with no entity ever eligible
choice_b: Yes, if the entity is more than 20%-owned by the earning licensee and specified statutory conditions are met
choice_c: Yes, to any unlicensed entity chosen by the licensee, without ownership restrictions
choice_d: No -- entity payments are barred even if the licensee owns 100% of the entity
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 43-40-25(b)(17) permits firm payment to an unlicensed entity more than 20%-owned by the earning licensee, under specified statutory conditions -- a narrow, ownership-gated carve-out, not an open-ended allowance.

question: Under O.C.G.A. § 43-40-25(b)(6), what must a licensee do regarding a referral fee or other thing of value received in connection with a transaction?
choice_a: Nothing -- referral fees need not be disclosed as long as they are reasonable in amount
choice_b: Disclose it verbally only, at or before closing
choice_c: Disclose it in writing to the principal, including commission paid to another broker for referring the principal
choice_d: Report it only to GREC, with no disclosure obligation to the principal
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 43-40-25(b)(6) requires written disclosure to the principal of any referral fee or thing of value received, including commission paid to another broker for referring the principal.

question: Under O.C.G.A. § 43-40-19(b), what must a broker do when an affiliated licensee's affiliation with the firm ends?
choice_a: Hold the license for up to 90 days pending an internal review
choice_b: Destroy the license, since it is no longer valid
choice_c: Nothing is required unless the licensee requests the transfer in writing
choice_d: Immediately forward the licensee's license to GREC or to the licensee's new broker
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 43-40-19(b) requires the broker to immediately forward the departing licensee's license to GREC or to the new broker.

question: A salesperson leaves Broker A intending to affiliate with Broker B. Under O.C.G.A. § 43-40-19, may the salesperson conduct licensed real estate activity for Broker B before the license transfer has been processed?
choice_a: No -- the departing licensee cannot act until the transfer is processed
choice_b: Yes -- the salesperson may begin working for Broker B immediately upon verbally notifying Broker A
choice_c: Yes -- as long as Broker B countersigns a temporary authorization letter
choice_d: Yes -- the 30-day grace period allows continued activity under either broker
explanation: Under O.C.G.A. § 43-40-19, a departing licensee cannot act on behalf of the new broker until the license transfer has actually been processed.

question: Under O.C.G.A. § 43-40-19(d), after a licensee's affiliation with a broker ends, may the former broker retain any right to compensation on pending transactions the licensee had been working?
choice_a: No -- all rights to compensation on pending transactions transfer automatically to the new broker
choice_b: Yes -- a former broker may retain compensation rights on enumerated pending transactions pursuant to a written agreement
choice_c: No -- a former broker forfeits any compensation claim the moment the affiliation ends, regardless of agreement
choice_d: Yes, but only if GREC pre-approves the arrangement in writing
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 43-40-19(d) allows a former broker to retain compensation rights on enumerated pending transactions via a written agreement, rather than automatically losing all claim to compensation.

question: Under O.C.G.A. § 43-40-18(c)(5), when is an individual licensee entitled to receive compensation for a licensed act?
choice_a: At any time, regardless of whether the licensee's license was assigned to the firm when the compensation was earned
choice_b: Only if the licensee has been affiliated with the firm for at least one full year
choice_c: Only when the licensee's license was assigned to the firm at the time the compensation was earned
choice_d: Only if the licensee personally attends the closing
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 43-40-18(c)(5) ties compensation eligibility to whether the licensee's license was assigned to the firm at the time the compensation was earned.

question: A salesperson negotiates a listing while affiliated with Firm X, then transfers her license to Firm Y before the commission is actually earned upon closing. Under O.C.G.A. § 43-40-18(c)(5), which firm's broker must ensure she is properly compensated?
choice_a: Firm X -- compensation always follows the firm where the listing was first taken, regardless of later transfers
choice_b: Either firm may pay her, at the salesperson's sole discretion
choice_c: Neither firm may pay her; only GREC may disburse compensation in this situation
choice_d: Firm Y -- compensation is tied to which firm the licensee's license was assigned to when the compensation was earned, not where the deal originated
explanation: Because O.C.G.A. § 43-40-18(c)(5) ties compensation to the firm the licensee's license was assigned to when the compensation was earned (i.e., at closing), Firm Y -- not Firm X where the listing originated -- is responsible.

question: Which of the following correctly summarizes a core principle running through Georgia's broker-salesperson compensation rules (O.C.G.A. §§ 43-40-18(c)(5), 43-40-19, 43-40-25(b)(8), (b)(17))?
choice_a: Compensation flow is tightly tied to licensure status and firm affiliation -- licensees must generally be paid by their own broker, only while properly affiliated and licensed, with narrow, specifically enumerated exceptions
choice_b: Georgia imposes no restrictions at all on who may pay or receive real estate compensation
choice_c: Only the qualifying broker of the largest firm involved in a transaction may ever be compensated
choice_d: Compensation rules in Georgia apply only to residential transactions, not commercial ones
explanation: Read together, O.C.G.A. §§ 43-40-18(c)(5), 43-40-19(b)-(d), and 43-40-25(b)(8),(17) show that Georgia ties compensation tightly to proper licensure and firm affiliation, generally requiring licensees to be paid by their own broker with only narrow, enumerated exceptions.
